# Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures

Yujian Liu   Li An   Zelin He   Jacob Helwig Affiliation: UC Santa
Barbara   Pennsylvania State University   LinkedIn    Jiabao Ji   Rohit
Jain   Siyu Zhu   Shiyu Chang
Email: [{yujianliu,li_an,jiabaoji,chang87}@ucsb.edu](mailto:)
Affiliation: UC Santa Barbara   Pennsylvania State University   LinkedIn

###### Abstract

Autonomous agents can increasingly propose ideas, modify code, and run
experiments, creating an opportunity to accelerate scientific discovery
using teams of collaborative AI researchers. To escape local minima in
the design space induced by common reasoning patterns, we propose to
encourage orthogonal exploration by constructing the team using agents
with varying expertise. However, realizing this design requires more
than diverse backgrounds. When experiments are costly, a team can test
only a limited number of ideas, thereby creating the need to balance
exploration and exploitation when selecting a subset of researchers to
propose and execute new experiments. Furthermore, each result should
shape what the team tries next. The team must decide where to deepen an
investigation, when to explore alternatives, and how to carry lessons
across researchers. We therefore ask how AI researchers with different
scientific backgrounds can build on one another’s findings and sustain
progress under a limited experimental budget. To address these
challenges, we build a team of persistent AI researchers, each grounded
in a different discipline, who keep private research histories, share
experimental evidence, and receive research opportunities through
adaptive allocation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design by
deploying the team to search for linear attention architectures at 150M
parameters. We then scale the team’s strongest discovery to 1.3B
parameters, where it outperforms GDN2 on language modeling, common-sense
reasoning, and synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks. In controlled
comparisons, removing any single organizational component from our
design yields markedly weaker discoveries: without disciplinary
backgrounds, the search plateaus early; without private histories,
researchers make less progress despite identical shared evidence; and
uniform selection falls short of adaptive allocation within the same
budget. Tracing the discovery shows researchers applying principles from
their own fields to refine one another’s ideas. These results suggest
that sustained autonomous discovery depends not only on stronger agents,
but also on who explores, what they remember, and how research effort is
allocated.

| --- |
|     |

## 1 Introduction

Autonomous research agents increasingly connect hypothesis generation,
implementation, and experimental evaluation into iterative discovery
processes ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Yamada et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2); [Schmidgall et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Novikov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4); [Lange et al., 2025](#bib.bib5); [Karpathy,
2026](#bib.bib19)). However, in well-developed fields, progress can
enter a local minimum when the explored region of the design space is
confined. Related efforts investigate how persistent experience and
collaboration can support scientific work across multiple agents and
repeated investigations ([Qu et al., 2026](#bib.bib6); [Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib8); [Swanson et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)). These
capabilities create a compelling opportunity to encourage diverse
exploration by assembling a team of AI researchers grounded in different
scientific fields, with distinct prior knowledge, conceptual frameworks,
and ways of reasoning, and having them work together to push the
state-of-the-art on the same open-ended problem. This allows the
researchers to leverage a mechanism suggested by one field to address a
limitation recognized in another. For example, advances in linear
attention have gained insights from fast-weight learning to build
memories that can correct stored associations ([Schlag et al.,
2021](#bib.bib18)). The potential value of such a team therefore lies
not only in generating more proposals, but in developing ideas through
complementary investigations.

Realizing this potential, however, requires more than assigning
researchers different backgrounds. When experiments are costly, a team
can test only a limited number of ideas and cannot pursue every
direction equally deeply. Which directions will prove productive is
uncertain, and due to the high cost of conducting an experiment,
exploration and exploitation must be balanced when selecting which of
the diverse hypotheses proposed by the team to test. Furthermore, an
early result may reveal a limitation that further work can address. Each
experiment therefore does more than test a proposal: it produces
evidence that can change what its author or another researcher tries
next. The team must use that evidence to decide where to deepen an
investigation and when to explore alternatives, while carrying useful
lessons across researchers and experiments. Existing demonstrations of
collaboration and search have not yet established what disciplinary
backgrounds and researchers’ own accumulated experience add to shared
evidence, or how research opportunities should be distributed across
such a team. With these challenges in mind, we therefore ask: _how can a
team of AI researchers with different scientific backgrounds build on
one another’s findings and sustain progress on open-ended research
problems under a limited experimental budget?_

![Refer to caption](2610.28887v1/intro-fig-v3.png)

Figure 1: Illustration of collaborative autoresearch. Sixteen research
agents with diverse scientific backgrounds collaborate on linear
attention architecture search. Starting from Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN2),
the team discovers Context-First DeltaNet (CFDN), which improves
performance across language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and
synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks.

To address these challenges, we propose an autoresearch pipeline that
brings together a team of persistent AI researchers, each initialized
with a different disciplinary profile containing domain knowledge,
mathematical tools, scientific insights, and ways to approach research
problems. The team conducts an iterative search in which each iteration
follows one proposal through independent review and, if approved,
implementation and evaluation, ending with its author reflecting on the
outcome. To make this process cumulative, researchers retain private
histories of their investigations while sharing proposals, outcomes, and
lessons with the team. This allows individual researchers to develop a
line of inquiry over time, while others can revisit its assumptions,
extend its mechanisms, or combine its findings with those from another
direction. As these lines of inquiry develop, an adaptive scheduler
balances further investment in researchers with strong empirical
contributions against opportunities for those whose potential is less
explored.

To ground this team in a problem that draws on different scientific
perspectives, we choose linear attention architecture discovery. Its
central modeling challenge is to retain and use sequence information
through a fixed-size recurrent state while maintaining model quality and
efficient computation ([Katharopoulos et al., 2020](#bib.bib9)). Recent
advances have explored connections between state-space models and
attention, delta-rule updates, channel-wise forgetting, and separately
controlled erasing and writing ([Dao and Gu, 2024](#bib.bib11); [Yang et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib12); [Yang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib10); [Team et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13); [Hatamizadeh et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)). These
developments illustrate how different perspectives can inform choices
about what to remember, how to revise stored information, and how to
retrieve it efficiently. Determining which of these choices improve
model performance requires implementing and training candidate
architectures. The cost of these experiments, in turn, limits how many
directions the team can pursue and how deeply it can investigate each
one. Building on prior demonstrations that agents can propose,
implement, and evaluate architectures ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib15);
[Pepe et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)), we therefore use this setting to study
how our heterogeneous team organization supports discovery under a
limited experimental budget.

We evaluate this organization at 150M model scale, using Gated
DeltaNet-2 (GDN2) as the baseline. Proposed candidates receive matched
training budgets and are evaluated on language modeling, common-sense
reasoning, and retrieval tasks. Our strongest discovery, _Context-First
DeltaNet_ (CFDN), adds a recurrent vector to GDN2’s matrix memory,
combining a query-independent contribution from the vector with a
query-dependent read from the matrix. We then scale it to 1.3B
parameters, where it improves performance in every evaluation category
over GDN2. To understand which organizational choices contribute to
these discoveries, we conduct controlled ablations on expert-background
conditioning, private longitudinal memory, adaptive researcher
selection, and evaluator design. Results show that providing
disciplinary profiles broadens the mechanisms explored and leads to
better architectures than those discovered without these profiles.
Private histories support more effective refinement of earlier ideas
beyond what is achieved with shared evidence alone. Adaptive selection
finds higher-scoring architectures than uniform selection within the
same number of research iterations. Optimizing solely for language
modeling, however, steers search toward improvements that transfer less
consistently across evaluations. We complement these comparisons by
tracing how ideas develop across researchers.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
provides an overview of the trajectories, which reveal connections
between researchers’ scientific backgrounds and the hypotheses they
pursue, as well as how they adopt and revise each other’s ideas using
shared experimental evidence.

To summarize, our contributions are threefold:

- •
  We build a framework for organizing autonomous research teams under
  limited compute, combining diverse scientific backgrounds, persistent
  memory, shared evidence, and adaptive allocation.
- •
  We discover improved linear attention architectures under matched
  training compute at 150M scale and evaluate the strongest at 1.3B
  scale.
- •
  We link organizational choices to discovery outcomes through
  controlled comparisons and trajectory analysis, providing guidance for
  designing autonomous research teams.

## 2 Methodology

We organize autonomous discovery as a collaboration among researchers
who bring different scientific perspectives to a shared problem,
encouraging orthogonal exploration of the design space. The team
develops through experience, makes each researcher’s findings useful to
others, and decides where to invest further effort.
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
gives an overview of our design. We first describe the researchers and
their individual and shared knowledge, then the iterative process
through which they develop and test ideas, where costly experiments
create a need to balance exploration and exploitation. Finally, we
define the experimental feedback that guides our search for linear
attention architectures.

![Refer to caption](2610.28887v1/method-v2.png)

Figure 2: Organization of the autonomous research team. (a) Sixteen
researchers have distinct scientific backgrounds and persistent
individual histories. Adaptive selection balances measured contributions
with opportunities for less-tested researchers. (b) A selected
researcher develops one proposal through review and, if approved,
implementation and experimentation, then reflects on its outcome. (c)
Proposals, outcomes, and their relationships form a shared body of
knowledge through which researchers build on one another’s work. Circled
numbers identify the four organizational factors studied in our
comparisons.

### 2.1 Scientific Perspectives and Accumulated Knowledge

In many well-researched areas, substantial progress is hindered by the
tendency of researchers to explore confined regions of an otherwise
broad space of potential designs, creating a local minimum. We therefore
propose to assemble our AI research team with different disciplinary
backgrounds to bring complementary concepts, assumptions, and diagnostic
tools to its investigation. Each researcher is an instance of the same
language model, with the same tools and a common description of the
problem, baseline, and experimental constraints.

Grounding researchers in scientific backgrounds. Each researcher
receives a disciplinary profile that develops three kinds of guidance:

- •
  Prior knowledge and mathematical tools: central objects, equations,
  assumptions, and representative literature that provide concrete
  mechanisms to reason with.
- •
  Scientific insights: when those mechanisms are useful, where familiar
  intuitions fail, and which apparently similar problems require
  different explanations.
- •
  Research habits: ways to decompose an unfamiliar problem, quantities
  to inspect, and counterexamples that could challenge a hypothesis.

For example, the Bayesian-filtering profile explains how prediction
errors should be interpreted relative to uncertainty and how to
distinguish isolated outliers from persistent changes. A
dynamical-systems profile emphasizes how repeated transitions preserve
or amplify perturbations. A streaming-algorithms profile asks which
queries a bounded summary must support. These perspectives suggest
different approaches to the same problem.
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Scientific profiles and researcher initialization ‣ Appendix C Organizational settings and analysis protocol ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
lists the full roster and example profiles.

Preserving individual experience. A profile is a starting point for
reasoning. Researchers may still develop their perspectives and insights
about how their area of expertise relates to the research problem. To
achieve that, each agent retains its session history and private
research notes across investigations, preserving hypotheses, the
reasoning behind earlier decisions, and reflections on their outcomes.
In addition to persisting these derived insights, this continuity allows
a researcher to revisit an unresolved question or revise an assumption.

Making findings useful to others. Private experience alone would leave
useful insights confined to their authors. All researchers therefore
have access to a shared record of proposals, reviews, experimental
results, and conclusions. It exposes both what was tried and why,
allowing researchers to extend a mechanism proposed by others,
reconsider an assumption, or combine findings from different
investigations. Accumulated findings are synthesized every 10 iterations
into shared lessons and unresolved questions. Individual histories and
shared knowledge thus support two forms of continuity: developing one’s
own reasoning and building on discoveries made elsewhere in the team.

### 2.2 An Iterative Process for Developing and Testing Ideas

With the initialized researchers, the team proposes and evaluates new
ideas to approach the problem in an iterative process. Each iteration
contains the following steps that turn existing knowledge into a new
investigation and return its findings to the team.

Step 1: Select a researcher. Although we would ideally allow all
researchers to propose and test diverse ideas in each iteration, this is
not tractable in most real-world research settings due to high
experimental costs. Therefore, in each iteration, we must first select
one researcher from the team to propose a new idea. With limited
experimental opportunities, repeatedly choosing recent winners can
overlook researchers whose ideas have not been sufficiently tested. We
therefore use discounted upper confidence bound (UCB)
selection ([Garivier and Moulines, 2011](#bib.bib20)) to balance
exploration and exploitation. Each completed iteration $`j`$ earns a
nonnegative reward $`r_{j}`$ for improving on the team’s best model
known when that iteration began.
Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Evaluating Architectures and Rewarding Research Progress ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
defines this reward in detail.

Specifically, let $`t`$ count completed iterations, $`t_{j}`$ be
iteration $`j`$’s completion ordinal, and $`\mathcal{J}_{i}`$ index the
$`i`$-th researcher’s completed iterations. For researcher $`i`$, we use
discount factor $`\gamma\in(0,1)`$ to compute an effective number of
observations $`N_{i}`$, mean reward $`\bar{r}_{i}`$, and selection score
$`A_{i}`$ as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
N_{i}(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}}\gamma^{t-t_{j}},\quad\bar{r}_{i}(t)=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}}\gamma^{t-t_{j}}r_{j}}{N_{i}(t)},\quad A_{i}(t)=\bar{r}_{i}(t)+c\sqrt{\frac{\log(\sum_{k}N_{k}(t))}{N_{i}(t)}}.
``` |  | (1) |

The researcher with the highest score $`A_{i}(t)`$ is selected for the
next iteration. The mean reward $`\bar{r}_{i}(t)`$ favors researchers
with stronger historical contributions, and the second term preserves
opportunities for less-tested researchers, with $`c`$ being a
hyperparameter controlling the strength of exploration. Intuitively, the
discount factor $`\gamma`$ assigns more weight to recent contributions,
thus giving researchers who perform well recently more continuity in
developing along their promising directions.

Step 2: Propose a hypothesis. Selection determines who investigates
next, but the researcher decides which scientific direction to pursue.
The selected researcher examines its own history and shared experimental
results to identify a limitation worth investigating. It may develop a
new mechanism or revise an earlier proposal, including one from another
researcher. The proposal states what should change, why that change
should help, and which experimental outcome would challenge the
hypothesis. For our linear attention architecture discovery, it
specifies the mathematical operations and their parameterization,
together with a parallelizable formulation suitable for training.

Step 3: Review the proposal. Before committing training compute, two
independent reviewers assess whether the proposed experiment is sound
and informative. A technical reviewer checks the mathematics and
computational feasibility. If these checks pass, a second reviewer
assesses novelty and research value in light of prior work and the
team’s findings. A rejection leads directly to reflection (Step 6);
otherwise, the reviews identify any issues to resolve before testing the
proposal.

Step 4: Refine the proposal. For a proposal that passes review, the
author revises its mathematical design in response to the critiques. The
author is responsible for resolving the reviewers’ critiques and
providing a detailed specification for implementation. If the critiques
cannot be addressed without replacing the central mechanism, the author
withdraws the proposal and proceeds to reflection.

Step 5: Implement, train, and evaluate. A separate implementation agent
translates the final specification into code and checks that it realizes
the intended computation. The implementation must pass integration and
speed checks before training. Specifically, we require the implemented
model’s per-step training time to be less than 1.2 times the baseline
GDN2 time to prevent architectures that degrade efficiency. Repairable
failures are returned to the implementer with diagnostics. Finally,
validated candidates are trained from scratch under matched training
compute, using the same training data, and evaluated with three metrics
defined in
Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Evaluating Architectures and Rewarding Research Progress ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures").

Step 6: Reflect and share. The proposing researcher revisits its
original hypothesis in light of the outcome, including rejection or
failure. Reviews, implementation, and experimental records are provided
to help it distinguish evidence about the mechanism from problems in
realizing or testing it. The researcher records what the outcome
supports, what remains unresolved, and what it suggests investigating
next. It updates its private notes for future reference and shares
generalizable lessons with other researchers. Completing this reflection
ends the iteration and updates the observations used for researcher
selection in future iterations.

### 2.3 Evaluating Architectures and Rewarding Research Progress

The evaluation metrics shape both the hypotheses researchers pursue and
the reward used by the selection rule. For linear attention discovery,
we seek improvements in general model capabilities that span different
tasks and scenarios. We therefore evaluate three complementary aspects
to measure progress on model quality (details in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Evaluation definitions and complete result tables ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")).

❶Language modeling measures next-token prediction with negative
log-likelihood $`L`$; lower is better. ❷ Common-sense reasoning measures
downstream task performance with mean accuracy $`Q`$; higher is better.
❸ Retrieval tests whether information remains accessible from context,
using an exact-continuation proxy $`R`$ on the synthetic
needle-in-a-haystack tasks; higher is better.

Model utility. To assess the utility of a specific trained model, we
measure its metrics $`(L_{x},Q_{x},R_{x})`$ and calculate its normalized
improvements over the baseline GDN2’s metrics $`(L_{0},Q_{0},R_{0})`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
U(x)=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{L_{0}-L_{x}}{s_{L}}+\frac{Q_{x}-Q_{0}}{s_{Q}}+\frac{R_{x}-R_{0}}{s_{R}}\right),
``` |  | (2) |

where $`(s_{L},s_{Q},s_{R})`$ are scales informed by metric variability
in preliminary experiments and remain fixed throughout all experiments.
Researchers see both the aggregated utility and individual metrics,
allowing them to inspect tradeoffs among the metrics.

Researcher reward. A high model utility may not indicate a new
contribution if a better model was already available. At the start of
iteration $`j`$, we therefore record the architecture with the highest
utility, including the baseline, as $`x_{j}^{\mathrm{ref}}`$. Candidate
architecture $`x_{j}`$ proposed in iteration $`j`$ then earns reward
$`r_{j}=\max\{0,\,U(x_{j})-U(x_{j}^{\mathrm{ref}})\}`$, which supplies
the reward used for selection. Rejected proposals or implementation
failures receive zero reward. Intuitively, this definition rewards
overall improvements compared to the best candidate so far, without
assigning negative rewards to unsuccessful attempts, thus encouraging
researchers to try out promising directions.

## 3 Experiments

Our experiments answer three questions: can the team discover useful
architectures; which organizational choices help in the
limited-iteration setting; and how do different researchers contribute
to a successful discovery? We first describe the experiment settings,
then evaluate the discovered architecture, compare research
organizations, and trace the development of the found architecture.

### 3.1 Experimental Setting

Research team. We use 16 researchers and a budget of 80 research
iterations. All agent roles use GPT-6 Astra with high reasoning effort
through the Codex harness. We allow a maximum of 8 researchers working
in parallel, while forcing their proposal stage to be sequential to
prevent repetition in proposed ideas. In the first 16 iterations, all
researchers are invoked exactly once, and further researcher selection
is based on the UCB rule.

Model backbones and search space. We search at approximately 150M
non-embedding parameters, and we scale the discovered best candidate to
1.3B parameters. We use GDN2 ([Hatamizadeh et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)) as
the baseline. Candidates can change the recurrent mixer’s memory
representation, update rule, readout, and parameterization, while
retaining the common depth, residual width, and feed-forward network. We
also compare with Gated DeltaNet (GDN) ([Yang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib10)) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) ([Team et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13)) using the same surrounding architecture.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Training and compute protocol ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
gives the dimensions and parameter-count convention at both scales.

Training data and budget. All models are trained from scratch on
FineWeb-Edu ([Penedo et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)). For all models, we
adjust their training tokens to match the total FLOPs of training GDN:
at 150M scale, we train GDN for 15B tokens; at 1.3B scale, we train GDN
for 100B tokens. More expensive architectures therefore receive fewer
training tokens. Following [Hatamizadeh et al. (2026)](#bib.bib14), all
models use the same optimizer hyperparameters and global batch size
(details in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Training and compute protocol ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")).

Final evaluation and search feedback. We evaluate models on language
modeling (LM), common-sense reasoning (CSR), synthetic
needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH), and, for 1.3B models, in-context real-world
retrieval (RWR) tasks. For LM, we report perplexity on WikiText
(Wiki.) ([Merity et al., 2016](#bib.bib22)) and LAMBADA (LMB.) ([Paperno
et al., 2016](#bib.bib23)). For CSR, we report the mean accuracy over
eight datasets ([Bisk et al., 2019](#bib.bib24); [Zellers et al.,
2019](#bib.bib25); [Sakaguchi et al., 2019](#bib.bib26); [Clark et al.,
2018](#bib.bib27); [Mihaylov et al., 2018](#bib.bib28); [Sap et al.,
2019](#bib.bib29); [Clark et al., 2019](#bib.bib30)). For NIAH, we use
four synthetic tasks (S-NIAH-1, 2, 3 and MK-NIAH) from RULER ([Hsieh et
al., 2024](#bib.bib31)). For in-context real-world retrieval, we report
mean accuracy over six datasets ([Arora et al., 2025](#bib.bib32);
[Rajpurkar et al., 2018](#bib.bib33); [Joshi et al., 2017](#bib.bib34);
[Kwiatkowski et al., 2019](#bib.bib35); [Dua et al., 2019](#bib.bib36)).

During search, we use a reduced suite to provide feedback: LM loss on
the same two datasets, a subset of 256 examples from each CSR dataset,
and 64 examples per NIAH task at each of 1K, 2K, and 4K context. We do
not evaluate RWR during search. The NIAH evaluation uses a
teacher-forced continuation proxy instead of answer generation.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Evaluation definitions and complete result tables ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
gives more details on evaluation.

### 3.2 Discovered Architecture and Validation at Larger Scale

The search run contains 63 candidate evaluations in 80 iterations.¹¹ 1
Rejected or failed proposals also count toward the budget, so it is not
a guarantee of 80 trained models. We select Context-First DeltaNet
(CFDN), the candidate with the highest search utility, and compare it
with GDN, KDA, and GDN2.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | Search | Full evaluation |  |  |  |
| Model | Tokens | Utility | Wiki. | LMB. | CSR | NIAH |
|  | \(B\) | $`U\uparrow`$ | ppl $`\downarrow`$ | ppl $`\downarrow`$ | acc $`\uparrow`$ | acc $`\uparrow`$ |
| GDN | 15.00 | -1.29 | 35.15 | 64.03 | 42.88 | 16.94 |
| KDA | 14.82 | -0.59 | 34.63 | 56.64 | 41.94 | 22.03 |
| GDN2 | 13.53 | 0.00 | 34.93 | 54.74 | 43.60 | 25.79 |
| CFDN | 13.53 | 1.04 | 33.84 | 52.33 | 43.29 | 29.76 |

Table 1: 150M comparison. $`U`$ is the aggregated search utility; CSR is
the mean of eight common-sense reasoning tasks; NIAH is the mean of four
synthetic retrieval tasks. Full results are in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Evaluation definitions and complete result tables ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures").

What was discovered? CFDN augments GDN2’s recurrent matrix memory with a
recurrent vector. The vector contributes the same context information to
every query, while the matrix supplies a query-dependent prediction.
Given the current token’s key, the memories jointly predict its value.
The defining change is how they learn from that prediction error: the
vector is updated first, and the matrix then fits the remaining error.
This gives shared information priority over query-specific correction.
The resulting update does not add notable compute over GDN2 and remains
compatible with efficient parallel training.
Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 How Researchers Develop the Discovered Architecture ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
explains how this mechanism is developed across researchers;
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 The discovered context-first recurrence ‣ Appendix D Architecture details ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
gives the full recurrence.

As shown in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Discovered Architecture and Validation at Larger Scale ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures"),
despite using the fewest training tokens, CFDN achieves a substantially
higher utility than all baselines. Specifically, it improves all three
search targets over GDN2: LM perplexity decreases from 12.21 to 11.90,
CSR accuracy rises from 44.48% to 44.63%, and retrieval rises from
28.91% to 50.00%. In terms of the final full evaluation, CFDN
outperforms all baselines on two language modeling tasks, and more
considerably on the NIAH tasks. Its CSR performance is slightly worse
than GDN2 but still better than GDN and KDA. These results demonstrate
that the search found a genuinely better architecture than the
baselines.

Validation at 1.3B. To validate whether the discovered architecture
remains effective at a larger scale, we train CFDN and all baselines at
around 1.3B parameters.
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Discovered Architecture and Validation at Larger Scale ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
compares the same four architectures under the GDN-100B reference
budget, using the full evaluation protocol.

At 1.3B, CFDN achieves the best performance in each evaluation category
among these models. It obtains the lowest perplexity on both LM datasets
and the highest mean CSR, NIAH, and real-world retrieval accuracy. This
validates that the discovered architecture remains effective at a larger
scale than the search region.

### 3.3 Which Organizational Choices Support Discovery?

A useful architecture does not by itself explain whether the team’s
organization helps discovery. We therefore compare the full system with
three variants, holding the agent model, iteration allowance,
per-candidate training budget, and search feedback fixed. ❶ *No
background* removes disciplinary profiles while retaining researcher
identities and their private histories. ❷ *Fresh memory* removes the
researchers’ private histories and notes between iterations, while
preserving their disciplinary profiles. ❸ *Uniform selection* replaces
the UCB-defined adaptive selection with a uniform selection that repeats
researchers in a fixed order. All variants retain access to shared
proposals, experimental results, and lessons, so each comparison
concerns a design beyond this common evidence.

The main and no-background runs start from scratch. To reduce variation
due to different initial discoveries, fresh-memory and uniform-selection
both reuse the main run’s first 16 iterations (one iteration per
researcher) and conduct 64 further iterations.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Organizational settings and analysis protocol ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
gives more details.

Figure 3: Candidate utility throughout the search. Points are evaluated
candidates; lines are the best found candidates up to an iteration.

Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Which Organizational Choices Support Discovery? ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
shows the utility of each candidate in the search process. The full
system discovers the strongest architecture in these comparisons: its
best utility is 1.04, versus 0.54 without backgrounds, 0.56 with fresh
memory, and 0.76 with uniform selection. The difference is also not
explained by completing more model evaluations: the main run contains 63
evaluated candidates, compared with 65-68 in the variants.

Interestingly, the main run’s strongest proposal appears at iteration
68, whereas the no-background run reaches its best utility at iteration
22 and does not improve it thereafter, which suggests that the diverse
scientific backgrounds help escape the local minima. The full system
also reaches higher utility than the fresh-memory and uniform-selection
runs, indicating that the private researcher memory and adaptive
allocation facilitate the team to make sustained progress on the
problem.

### 3.4 How Does the Search Objective Steer Discoveries?

We next study how the choice of search objective affects the
architectures discovered. We compare the three-target objective with an
independent LM-only search, retaining the same researcher profiles,
private memory, adaptive selection rule, and experimental budget. The
LM-only condition uses the same WikiText and LAMBADA perplexity but
excludes CSR and NIAH from the objective. Each condition selects its
strongest candidate using its own objective.

| Search objective | Wiki. | LMB. | CSR | NIAH |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | ppl $`\downarrow`$ | ppl $`\downarrow`$ | acc $`\uparrow`$ | acc $`\uparrow`$ |
| LM only | 34.59 | 46.40 | 42.25 | 26.73 |
| LM $`+`$ CSR $`+`$ NIAH | 33.84 | 52.33 | 43.29 | 29.76 |

Table 3: Effect of the search objective. Full evaluation of the model
discovered at 150M scale.

Table [3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.4 How Does the Search Objective Steer Discoveries? ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
compares the full evaluation of two models at 150M scale. As can be
observed, LM-only search achieves a substantially lower perplexity on
LAMBADA, while three-target search yields stronger results on the other
metrics. These results indicate that objective choice matters for
discovery: gains under an LM-only objective may not extend to all
capabilities of interest. This is relevant to popular autoresearch
systems guided by LM quality, such as [Karpathy (2026)](#bib.bib19),
which uses validation bits per byte as its objective. Although
perplexity captures broad predictive performance, averaging over many
token predictions can dilute the influence of the few answer tokens that
determine success in the tasks of interest, such as retrieval and
common-sense reasoning, motivating explicit evaluation of these
capabilities.

### 3.5 How Researchers Develop the Discovered Architecture

Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
traces CFDN’s development through contributions from four researchers. A
researcher grounded in linear attention introduces a recurrent context
vector alongside GDN2’s matrix memory, building on affine-memory
precedent ([Zuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)). Another researcher learns
the address origin that determines what this vector represents. A
researcher with expertise in adaptive filtering then normalizes the
correction by the translated address’s energy, showing how disciplinary
knowledge can refine a colleague’s mechanism.

The next revision updates the matrix before the context vector,
improving LM perplexity but weakening CSR and retrieval. A researcher
with a background in predictive representations uses this tradeoff to
reconsider which memory should absorb the prediction error first. It
then switches to updating shared context before the matrix, which
produces CFDN. Thus, the team uses a degraded result to guide a
subsequent improvement, rather than simply retaining successful
proposals.

## 4 Related Work

Autonomous research agents. A growing line of work automates the
iterative research process from hypothesis to experiment, through fixed
pipelines from idea generation to written paper ([Lu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Schmidgall et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)), agentic tree
search ([Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)), or evolutionary search with
the language model as the mutation operator ([Novikov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4); [Lange et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)). In these works, a
single agent or a fixed pipeline proposes every candidate.

Other work organizes a team of researchers around a shared scientific
problem. These teams differ in how they are composed, what each member
retains and what the team shares, and how research opportunities are
distributed. VirSci, ASCollab, and ScienceClaw ([Su et al.,
2025](#bib.bib37); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib8); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib38)) give agents distinct backgrounds, personas, or
scientific profiles. CORAL ([Qu et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)), ASCollab, and
ScienceClaw keep long-running agents with their own histories and a
shared record, whereas AgentRxiv ([Schmidgall and Moor,
2025](#bib.bib39)) starts a fresh laboratory instance per project that
reads a shared archive of earlier papers. However, none compares teams
with and without different backgrounds on the outcomes of implementing,
training, and evaluating what they propose, or tests whether private
memory adds anything once findings are shared.

Adaptive allocation itself is not new, but no existing work both gives
researchers different backgrounds and allocates opportunities among them
adaptively. The Virtual Lab ([Swanson et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)) decides
which specialist takes an agenda item, ShinkaEvolve ([Lange et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5)) decides which language model performs the next
mutation, SwarmResearch ([Virk et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)) decides which
branch of the search to extend, and Economy of Minds ([Qi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib41)) decides which agent acts next in a task. Each of them
chooses an operator or a candidate to advance. In our setting, the
decision is which researcher proposes and tests the next idea, and
because each researcher brings its own background and record of what it
has tried and learned, that choice determines what evidence the team
will have next. No prior team of researchers with different backgrounds
makes this decision adaptively.

Autonomous research has also been applied to architecture design.
NADER ([Yang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib42)) coordinates fixed-role agents
that propose changes to a tree of prior modifications. AIRA-Compose and
AIRA-Design ([Pepe et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)) pool designs from
independent search agents, and ASI-Arch ([Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib15)) runs a researcher, engineer, and analyst pipeline
over linear attention architectures and reports that discoveries grow
with compute. These systems use fixed-role workflows or independent
agent searches; we instead fix the experimental budget and vary the
organization, comparing who proposes, what they retain and share, who
receives the next opportunity, and what counts as progress.

Linear attention. Linear attention replaces the key-value cache of
softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state ([Katharopoulos et
al., 2020](#bib.bib9)), and subsequent designs mainly differ in what the
state remembers, how stored information is revised, and how it is
retrieved. On what to remember, most designs keep a matrix of key–value
associations, while Titans ([Behrouz et al., 2024](#bib.bib43)) replaces
it with a network learned at inference. On how to revise, RetNet ([Sun
et al., 2023](#bib.bib17)) decays the state at a fixed rate, GLA and
Mamba-2 ([Yang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib44); [Dao and Gu,
2024](#bib.bib11)) make the decay input-dependent, DeltaNet ([Yang et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib12)) replaces additive writes with delta-rule
correction, GDN and KDA ([Yang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib10); [Team et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13)) combine the delta rule with learned and fine-grained
gating, and GDN2 ([Hatamizadeh et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)) separates
erasing from writing with channel-wise gates. On how to retrieve,
MesaNet ([von Oswald et al., 2026](#bib.bib45)) solves the regression to
optimality at every step, and Parallax ([Zuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib46))
restores the intercept of the underlying regression. Each of these works
changes one or two choices along these axes, and the space they leave
open is large, which makes linear attention architecture discovery a
natural problem for an autonomous research team.

## 5 Conclusion

We study how to organize autonomous researchers for cumulative discovery
under limited experimental budgets. Our framework combines diverse
scientific backgrounds, persistent memory, shared evidence, and adaptive
allocation of research opportunities. Applied to linear attention, the
team discovered CFDN, which improves over GDN2 at two scales.
Organizational comparisons and research trajectories highlight the
importance of heterogeneous agents, adaptive allocation, and shared
experimental records. Together, these results suggest that sustained
autonomous discovery depends on how a team learns from experiments and
decides which ideas to pursue next.

### Acknowledgements

The UCSB team acknowledges support from the National Science Foundation
(NSF) Grant IIS2338252.

### AI use statement

Our use of AI falls into two categories. First, AI-driven research is
the subject of this work. The LLM agents in our system propose and
refine architectural hypotheses, review proposals, implement methods,
interpret experimental results, and share findings. These activities are
part of the research methodology described and evaluated in the paper.

Second, we used AI tools to assist the authors in developing and
debugging the autoresearch framework, inspecting agent trajectories to
diagnose issues in the research workflow, and polishing the manuscript.
The authors reviewed these contributions and take responsibility for the
final content of the paper and its associated artifacts.

### Ethics statement

This work studies autonomous research in model architecture design using
existing training corpora and evaluation benchmarks, without recruiting
human participants. The principal ethical concerns involve research
integrity: agents may generate incorrect claims, overlook prior work, or
optimize evaluation metrics without improving broader capabilities. We
retain records of proposals, reviews, implementations, and experimental
outcomes to support scrutiny, and use implementation checks and
evaluation across multiple capabilities to assess proposed improvements.
These safeguards do not guarantee correctness or novelty.

### Reproducibility statement

We document model configurations, training hyperparameters, data
preparation, and FLOP-matched budget allocation in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Training and compute protocol ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures").
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Evaluation definitions and complete result tables ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
specifies the search and full-evaluation protocols, including example
selection, decoding settings, scoring rules, and per-dataset results.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Organizational settings and analysis protocol ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
details researcher initialization, information access, memory
conditions, adaptive allocation, and the shared starting point used in
organizational comparisons; it also reproduces one complete researcher
profile.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Architecture details ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
provides the discovered architecture’s recurrence, parameterization, and
initialization.

## Appendix A Training and compute protocol

Tables [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix A Training and compute protocol ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")

summarize the model configurations and training hyperparameters,
respectively.

| Setting                       | Search scale    | Large-scale comparison |
|-------------------------------|-----------------|------------------------|
| Blocks                        | 8               | 18                     |
| Residual / FFN width          | 1,024 / 4,096   | 2,304 / 6,208          |
| GDN2 recurrent heads          | $`8\times 128`$ | $`16\times 128`$       |
| GDN2 non-embedding parameters | 155,322,432     | 1,302,640,416          |
| GDN2 total parameters         | 220,858,432     | 1,450,096,416          |
| Output gate                   | Sigmoid         | Sigmoid                |
| Vocabulary size               | 32,000          | 32,000                 |

the outer backbone is fixed within each scale. Scale labels exclude the

and the output projection is included in reference FLOPs.

|                              |                     |                     |
|------------------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| Hyperparameter               | Search scale        | 1.3B scale          |
| Optimizer                    | AdamW               | AdamW               |
| Peak learning rate           | $`4\times 10^{-4}`$ | $`4\times 10^{-4}`$ |
| Minimum learning rate        | $`4\times 10^{-5}`$ | $`4\times 10^{-5}`$ |
| Adam $`\beta_{1},\beta_{2}`$ | 0.9, 0.95           | 0.9, 0.95           |
| Weight decay                 | 0.1                 | 0.1                 |
| Gradient clipping norm       | 1.0                 | 1.0                 |
| Warmup fraction              | 1%                  | 1%                  |
| Learning-rate decay          | Cosine              | Cosine              |
| Context length               | 4,096               | 4,096               |
| Global batch (sequences)     | 512                 | 512                 |
| Tokens per optimizer update  | 2,097,152           | 2,097,152           |
| Microbatch (sequences)       | 8                   | 4                   |
| Accumulation steps           | 8                   | 2                   |
| Training seed                | 3407                | 3407                |
| Compute anchor (GDN tokens)  | 15B                 | 100B                |

Table 5: Training hyperparameters. The optimizer settings and global
batch size are shared by all architectures. Microbatch size denotes the
sequences processed per device in one forward/backward pass.

Common small-scale data stream. The search corpus is prepared once from
24 FineWeb-Edu source shards with the TinyLlama tokenizer. Within each
shard, tokenized documents are concatenated and packed into 4,097-ID
blocks, yielding 4,096 input–target positions per sequence. Long
documents span multiple blocks; only each shard’s final incomplete block
is discarded. One saved permutation determines the global sequence
order. Each candidate consumes the first $`T(x)/4096`$ sequences of that
same order, without reshuffling after budget selection. An optimizer
update advances by 512 sequences.

Baseline parameterization. GDN2 uses separate full projections for
queries, keys, values, and channel-wise erase and write gates. Query,
key, and value projections are followed by causal depthwise convolutions
of width four and SiLU; queries and keys are L2-normalized. Decay and
output-gate preactivations use two linear maps with bottleneck width
128. The recurrent read is RMS-normalized per head, multiplied by a
sigmoid output gate, and projected back to the residual stream. Our KDA
comparison shares these surrounding components and initialization but
uses one scalar erase/write gate per head; GDN additionally uses scalar
rather than channel-wise state decay. The architectural differences are
therefore confined to the recurrent mechanisms within a common
surrounding backbone, rather than unrelated released model recipes.

### A.1 Architectural reference FLOPs and practical constraints

For training-compute budget $`\mathcal{C}`$, reference FLOPs per token
$`F(x)`$, and $`B`$ processed token positions per optimizer update,
search allocates $`T(x)=B\lfloor\mathcal{C}/(BF(x))\rfloor`$ tokens.
Rounding down to complete updates keeps each candidate within the
nominal budget.

Let $`P_{\mathrm{proj}}`$ count active dense and convolutional weights,
and let $`C_{\mathrm{mem}}`$ and $`C_{\mathrm{extra}}`$ denote forward
reference arithmetic per token for memory computation and any other
substantial tensor operations. The allocation uses

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F(x)=6P_{\mathrm{proj}}+3\bigl(C_{\mathrm{mem}}+C_{\mathrm{extra}}\bigr).
``` |  | (3) |

Input-embedding lookup is excluded; the language-model output projection
is included. Biases, normalization scales, and static parameters are
inventoried separately from projection weights. Repeated uses of a
shared projection are charged for their additional computation. For
custom operators, the forward count is multiplied by three as a uniform
training-cost approximation.

The general counting rule is to include projections and memory
computation, while excluding ordinary token-local scalar/vector
processing. Memory reads, contractions, outer-product updates, and
transformations of stored state are counted. Ordinary activations,
normalization, scalar/vector gates, residual additions, embedding
lookup, loss computation, optimizer steps, communication, and
checkpointing are excluded. This is a consistent architectural proxy,
not a hardware instruction count.

The proposer derives the breakdown, the technical reviewer checks it,
and the author’s revision resolves disagreements. Automated checks
measure the implemented weight inventory. A mismatch receives one
implementer recheck before the measured counts determine the projection
term; the custom-operation terms remain those approved in scientific
review. Neither parameter counting nor finite training alone proves that
an arbitrary implementation faithfully realizes the specification.

For the small GDN compute anchor, $`F=1{,}037{,}893{,}632`$ FLOPs/token,
giving $`\mathcal{C}=1.556840448\times 10^{19}`$ FLOPs. GDN2 costs
$`1{,}150{,}353{,}408`$ FLOPs/token and receives 6,453 updates; CFDN
costs $`1{,}150{,}500{,}864`$ FLOPs/token and receives 6,452.

Practical speed is checked separately. Candidate optimizer-step time
must be at most $`1.2\times`$ the baseline measured on the same
hardware. During training, the candidate must reach 25%, 50%, 75%, and
100% of its own allocation within $`1.2\times`$ the corresponding
baseline elapsed times. These checks can reject an implementation even
when its analytical compute is small. Ordinary implementation repairs
receive at most three rounds of validation and repair and six active
hours; infrastructure failures do not count as scientific failures.
These constraints define the implemented search space and must be
retained in organizational comparisons.

## Appendix B Evaluation definitions and complete result tables

Search suite. WikiText-2 (Wiki.) uses 62 documents scored through
independent rolling 4K windows, totaling 322,149 scored tokens. LAMBADA
(LMB.) uses 5,153 examples and scores their final-word continuations,
totaling 8,808 tokens. We average the two token-mean negative
log-likelihoods equally before exponentiation.

CSR uses 256 fixed examples from each of PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande,
ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA, Social IQa, and BoolQ. Option
likelihoods follow the frozen zero-shot requests. HellaSwag uses
character-normalized accuracy; the other tasks use raw accuracy. The
reported $`Q`$ is the unweighted mean over these eight tasks.

Retrieval uses S-NIAH-1, S-NIAH-2, S-NIAH-3, and MK-NIAH-1, with 64
fixed examples at each of 1K, 2K, and 4K, totaling 768. The evaluator
reveals the first continuation token and teacher-forces the rest. An
example passes only if every remaining answer token is the model’s
argmax. The first token is not scored. The reported $`R`$ averages the
12 task/length cells equally. This proxy does not require autoregressive
generation.

Full evaluation. The full protocol uses all examples in the selected
LM/CSR datasets and generated-answer NIAH scoring. NIAH contains 500
frozen requests per task/length cell: S-NIAH-1/2 at 1K, 2K, 4K, and 8K,
and S-NIAH-3/MK-NIAH-1 at 1K, 2K, and 4K, for 7,000 requests in 14
cells. All models receive the same requests. Generation is greedy, with
at most 128 new tokens and early stopping at EOS. We use batch size
eight, BF16, and cached decoding. The RULER scorer checks whether each
reference answer appears in the generated text as a case-insensitive
substring and averages the fraction of references recovered per request;
it does not require the entire generated string to equal the answer. The
NIAH mean weights all cells equally.

Real-world retrieval at 1.3B. We use the released BASED/JRT
cloze-completion suite ([Arora et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)): SWDE, SQuAD,
FDA, TriviaQA, Natural Questions (NQ), and DROP. This suite is used only
for final evaluation of the 1.3B models and does not enter search
feedback or utility. The nominal context length is 2K. We retain the
released preprocessing and its exclusions for empty or single-character
primary answers, leaving 12,077 examples: 1,067, 2,977, 1,101, 1,688,
3,157, and 2,087 in the dataset order above. Context is cropped before
appending the cloze query; two final NQ prompts consequently contain
2,062 tokens.

Evaluation is zero-shot, with no chat template or context repetition.
Greedy cached decoding generates at most 48 tokens, stopping at a
newline or EOS, in BF16 batches of up to eight examples of equal input
length. An answer is correct if an accepted reference appears in the
generated text as a case-insensitive substring. We report the unweighted
mean of the six dataset accuracies.

Search-scale reporting.

## Appendix C Organizational settings and analysis protocol

### C.1 Scientific profiles and researcher initialization

The team uses 16 fixed disciplinary profiles. Each is a self-contained
document of approximately 2,000–2,300 words, combining a field’s
mathematical foundations, design judgments, diagnostic practices, and
primary references.
Table [13](#A3.T13 "Table 13 ‣ C.1 Scientific profiles and researcher initialization ‣ Appendix C Organizational settings and analysis protocol ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
summarizes the different research questions these documents foreground.
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 An exact researcher profile ‣ Appendix C Organizational settings and analysis protocol ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
reproduces the complete Bayesian-filtering profile supplied to one
researcher. Only the focal linear attention profile is written
specifically about the target architecture family.

At initialization, each researcher receives one profile, the common
problem statement, and access to shared references covering the
baseline, prior work, and experimental constraints. Its conversation,
private notebook, and earlier proposal dossiers preserve individual
experience as the search proceeds. At each new assignment, the
researcher additionally receives a summary of previous results, ongoing
investigations, and consolidated shared lessons, with access to the
underlying records. The fixed profile therefore supplies an initial
technical perspective, while private and shared evidence can change the
researcher’s subsequent judgments.

|  Scientific perspective |  Organizing question or distinction |
|----|----|
|  Conditional routing and adaptive computation |  When should state change, which path should act, and when is further computation worthwhile? |
|  Multiscale and hierarchical recurrence |  How should clocks, temporal boundaries, and communication represent phenomena at different rates? |
|  Stable, switched, and non-normal dynamics |  Which distinctions survive input-driven transitions, and when do perturbations amplify? |
|  Multiplicative operators and automata |  What computations can input-selected operators express through composition? |
|  Parallel and I/O-aware recurrent design |  Which algebraic structure permits efficient execution once state traffic and differentiation are counted? |
|  Streaming sketches and mergeable summaries |  Which queries must bounded state support, and how does error compose across updates and merges? |
|  Cache policies and memory hierarchies |  What deserves residency, when should it move, and when is a stored copy no longer useful? |
|  Differentiable computers and neural data structures |  Do learned addressing, allocation, and traversal retain their meaning under repeated operations? |
|  Predictive representations and information bottlenecks |  Which distinctions in history matter for future predictions, and which can be discarded? |
|  Bayesian filtering and regime change |  How should uncertainty determine correction, and how can an outlier be distinguished from a change of regime? |
|  Continual memory and consolidation |  How can new information be acquired without overwriting useful prior structure? |
|  Associative and sparse adaptive memory |  How do retrieval, residual competition, and allocation interact under finite capacity? |
|  Vector-symbolic structured memory |  Which binding, superposition, and cleanup operations preserve compositional meaning? |
|  Tensor, spectral, and low-rank operator memory |  What state rank preserves distinctions needed by future computations? |
|  Online recurrent learning and eligibility traces |  How can delayed credit be assigned with bounded storage and causal updates? |
|  Linear attention and recurrent matrix memory |  How should a fixed-size matrix state read, write, correct, and forget while supporting parallel training? |

Table 13: The 16 scientific perspectives. Each row summarizes one
profile’s organizing question; it is not a prescribed candidate
mechanism or an exclusive research territory.

### C.2 Research protocol and analysis details

Proposal and review details. Each proposal specifies its hypothesis,
expected benefit, and a falsifying outcome, together with state
equations, parameterization, a parallelizable training formulation, and
an analytical compute breakdown. For lineage analysis, it identifies one
primary scientific precursor and may cite other influences; this
attribution does not require retaining the precursor’s architecture.
Technical review precedes contextual review. Both reviewers are blind to
the author’s identity and the other review. The technical reviewer
assesses the proposal without the shared research history, while the
contextual reviewer uses that history to assess duplication and research
value. The original researcher then resolves correctable issues into the
revised specification.

Memory and information access. The persistent condition preserves the
originating researcher’s conversation and notebook across iterations.
The fresh condition preserves them only within one iteration, including
proposal revision and terminal reflection. It still receives shared
proposals, results, published lessons, and the shared result summary.
Reviewers and implementers use task-specific sessions in both
conditions. The evidence available at reflection includes reviews,
source code, records of implementation attempts, training logs, and
evaluation artifacts. A director consolidates shared lessons after every
ten completed reflections; it does not select the next researcher. Agent
tools include web search and a numerical Python environment. Model
source and GPU execution belong to the implementation role, rather than
the proposing researcher.

Allocation and displayed ranks. The adaptive policy uses
$`\gamma=2^{-1/32}`$ and $`c=0.25`$ in
Eq. ([1](#S2.E1 "In 2.2 An Iterative Process for Developing and Testing Ideas ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")).
An observation’s weight therefore halves after 32 completed reflections,
without changing the recorded model utility or the reward originally
assigned to its researcher. Researchers with unresolved investigations
are ineligible. Uniform selection repeats the first-round researcher
order and waits if the next researcher is busy; it does not skip ahead
according to completion time or reward. In the shared-prefix experiment,
this gives every researcher four new assignments. Ties in the adaptive
comparison use a stable researcher ordering common to the continuation
arms.

The shared result summary displays numeric utility for every complete
comparable endpoint. It shows overall top-five ranks only for candidates
whose regressions relative to GDN2 do not exceed 0.01 NLL, 0.2 CSR
percentage points, or 2 retrieval percentage points. A candidate outside
these tolerances retains its numerical utility and a marker naming the
regressing target. This display rule does not filter scheduler rewards
or the highest-utility reference used for researcher credit
(Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Evaluating Architectures and Rewarding Research Progress ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")).

Common first-round evidence. The fresh-memory and uniform-selection runs
import the main run’s first 16 investigations. Their proposals, reviews,
specifications, implementation evidence, and outcomes are identical at
the branch. Uniform selection retains the reconstructed private
conversations and notes; fresh memory creates a new private researcher
session for every subsequent iteration. Both can read the common shared
evidence, including published reflections and lessons, and conduct 64
new iterations.

Recorded parent relationships.
Table [14](#A3.T14 "Table 14 ‣ C.2 Research protocol and analysis details ‣ Appendix C Organizational settings and analysis protocol ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
summarizes relationships declared in proposals. We count a parent–child
pair only when the parent is an earlier candidate, excluding GDN2. A
pair is eligible for the utility comparison when both models have
complete evaluations; an improvement means strictly higher child
utility. For cross-researcher links, we count proposals whose declared
candidate parent belongs to a different researcher, including proposals
without a completed evaluation. The denominators therefore differ. These
are counts of declared relationships and measured outcomes, rather than
annotations of mechanism novelty or proof of knowledge transfer.

| Condition |  Completed evaluations |  Higher utility than parent |  Cross-researcher parent links |
|----|----|----|----|
| Main | 63 | 9/41 | 41/54 |
| No background | 67 | 12/42 | 41/57 |
| Fresh memory | 65 | 5/32 | 36/44 |
| Uniform selection | 68 | 15/46 | 38/57 |

## Appendix D Architecture details

### D.1 The discovered context-first recurrence

We describe Context-First DeltaNet (CFDN), introduced in
Sections [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Discovered Architecture and Validation at Larger Scale ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures")
and [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 How Researchers Develop the Discovered Architecture ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures").
GDN2 stores information in a recurrent matrix and retrieves it through a
query-dependent read. CFDN adds a recurrent context vector that
contributes the same additive term to every query. This gives the memory
two ways to represent information: a shared context contribution and an
address-dependent contribution from the matrix.

The central idea is how these two memories learn from a prediction
error. At each token, they jointly predict the gated value. CFDN
corrects the context vector first, then updates the matrix using the
error that remains. This gives shared context priority and encourages
the matrix to represent corrections beyond what context already
explains.

Correct context before fitting the remaining error. For one head, let
$`\mathbf{S}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d_{v}}`$ be the matrix memory
and $`\mathbf{m}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}`$ the context vector, both
initialized to zero. Let
$`\mathbf{q}_{t},\mathbf{k}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}`$ be the normalized
query and key, $`\mathbf{v}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}`$ the value, and
$`\mathbf{b}_{t}\in(0,1)^{d_{k}}`$ and
$`\mathbf{w}_{t}\in(0,1)^{d_{v}}`$ the sigmoid erase and write gates. As
in GDN2, a channel-wise log-decay $`\mathbf{g}_{t}`$ first acts on the
matrix:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{\mathbf{S}}_{t}=\operatorname{Diag}(\exp\mathbf{g}_{t})\mathbf{S}_{t-1}.
``` |  | (4) |

The context vector has no passive decay. Denote the matrix’s write and
prediction addresses by $`\mathbf{a}_{t}`$ and $`\mathbf{e}_{t}`$, the
context weight by $`c`$, and the correction normalizer by
$`\kappa_{t}`$. Their construction is given below. The context
contribution to the predictor uses the mean erase gate,
$`\beta_{t}=d_{k}^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{d_{k}}b_{t,j}`$. The update has four
steps:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\bm{\delta}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\underbrace{\mathbf{w}_{t}\odot\mathbf{v}_{t}}_{\text{gated value}}-\underbrace{\left(\bar{\mathbf{S}}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{t}+c\beta_{t}\mathbf{m}_{t-1}\right)}_{\text{joint prediction}},`$ |  | (5) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbf{m}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbf{m}_{t-1}+\frac{c}{\kappa_{t}}\bm{\delta}_{t},`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\bm{\delta}_{t}^{\mathrm{rem}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbf{w}_{t}\odot\mathbf{v}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{S}}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{t}-c\beta_{t}\mathbf{m}_{t},`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\bar{\mathbf{S}}_{t}+\frac{\mathbf{a}_{t}}{\kappa_{t}}\left(\bm{\delta}_{t}^{\mathrm{rem}}\right)^{\top}.`$ |  |  |

The first line measures what the two memories fail to predict together.
The second assigns part of that error to shared context. The third
recomputes the error after this context correction, while keeping the
matrix fixed. Only then does the fourth line update the matrix.

Equivalently, the error passed to the matrix is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bm{\delta}_{t}^{\mathrm{rem}}=\left(1-\frac{c^{2}\beta_{t}}{\kappa_{t}}\right)\bm{\delta}_{t}.
``` |  | (6) |

Thus, the two corrections can be combined algebraically into a single
rank-one update of the augmented memory, retaining compatibility with
parallel chunkwise training.

Choose what the shared context represents. CFDN learns a reference
address, or origin, $`\bm{\mu}`$ for each head. The matrix reads and
writes relative to this origin. It also learns a scalar $`\rho`$ that
controls the relative weighting of the matrix and context coordinates:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho=\frac{\sigma(\theta)}{8},\qquad s=\sqrt{1-\rho},\qquad c=\sqrt{\rho},\qquad\bm{\mu}=\frac{\mathbf{u}}{8\sqrt{1+\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^{2}}},
``` |  | (7) |

where $`\theta\in\mathbb{R}`$ and $`\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}`$
are learned parameters. Unlike the recurrent context vector, these
parameters are fixed across tokens. The matrix addresses are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{a}_{t}=s(\mathbf{k}_{t}-\bm{\mu}),\qquad\mathbf{e}_{t}=\mathbf{b}_{t}\odot\mathbf{a}_{t}.
``` |  | (8) |

The write address determines where the matrix stores a correction; the
prediction address additionally applies GDN2’s channel-wise erase gate.
Translation changes the address energy, so CFDN scales both corrections
using

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\kappa_{t}=1+(1-\rho)\left(\lVert\bm{\mu}\rVert^{2}-2\mathbf{k}_{t}^{\top}\bm{\mu}\right).
``` |  | (9) |

This compensates for the energy change caused by translation and gives
$`\kappa_{t}=1`$ when $`\bm{\mu}=\mathbf{0}`$.

After updating both memories, the raw readout is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{o}_{t}=\frac{s\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}(\mathbf{q}_{t}-\bm{\mu})+c\mathbf{m}_{t}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}.
``` |  | (10) |

The context term contributes equally to every query, while the matrix
term varies with the query’s displacement from the learned origin. At
$`\mathbf{q}_{t}=\bm{\mu}`$, the matrix contribution vanishes, so
passive matrix decay alone leaves this readout unchanged. Subsequent
corrections can still change its readout through $`\mathbf{m}_{t}`$.

We initialize $`\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}`$ and $`\theta=-\log 15`$, giving
$`\rho=1/128`$. The parameterization ensures
$`\lVert\bm{\mu}\rVert<1/8`$ and $`0<\rho<1/8`$. Our models use
$`d_{k}=d_{v}=128`$ and retain GDN2’s surrounding components: the
query/key/value projections and short convolutions, independent
erase/write projections, and per-head RMS normalization followed by
sigmoid output gating and the output projection suggested by [Team et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib13).
````
